extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, journalists, copyeditors, and communicators writing about transgender people (primarily U.S. context)
extracted.subtask_description: A style guide for respectful, bias-aware language and editorial choices when writing about transgender and gender-diverse people, with usage rules, examples, and contextual guidance. Focuses on inclusive wording, pronouns, anatomy, identity, and reporting ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgender is an adjective.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: transgender people; a transgender person; transgender issues. Avoid: transgenders; the transgendered; writing about transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'transgender' grammatically as an adjective rather than a noun or label; follow provided example phrasings and explicit 'avoid' list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgender is not a sexual orientation.
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct terms in a trans context: gender; gender identity and expression. Incorrect terms in a trans context: sexual identity; sexuality. Avoid questions like 'Are you straight, gay, lesbian, bisexual, or transgender (pick one)?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate gender identity with sexual orientation; use the proper terminology (gender/gender identity) when discussing trans people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition is the correct word for the social and/or medical process of publicly living into one’s true gender or absence of gender.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: Chris transitioned at age 32; the transition process. Avoid: Chris is transgendering; Chris had a sex change; Chris had 'the surgery'; Chris became a woman; Chris changed genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the diversity of transition pathways (social, medical, none). Avoid implying there's a single 'correct' or 'complete' transition (avoid phrases like 'fully transition' or 'finish transitioning'); transition is not required to be trans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgender does not refer only to binary-identified trans women and men.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: transgender people; people of all genders. Avoid (in reference to all trans people): transgender women and men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that transgender includes non-binary people. When specificity is needed, use phrases such as 'trans and non-binary people' or alternatives listed. Note provided discussion about 'trans' vs 'transgender' and variants like 'trans+' and 'trans*'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender nonconforming and non-binary are not synonyms.
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender nonconforming generally refers to expression that doesn't match stereotypes; non-binary refers to identity not exclusively man or woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms accurately and avoid using umbrella terms carelessly; if in doubt be descriptive and specific about who is being discussed. Avoid terms with negative connotations (e.g., 'gender deviant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgender is a descriptive term, not (usually) a gender and not always an identity.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: transgender people; transgender history or identity. Avoid: people who identify as transgender; Are you a man, a woman, or transgender (pick one)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that many people may identify as a woman/man without emphasizing 'transgender' as their gender; treat 'transgender' like 'cisgender' — descriptive rather than a standalone gender category in most contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language that reduces people to their birth-assigned sex or their (assumed) biology.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: birth-assigned sex; sex assigned at birth; gender associated with one’s sex assigned at birth. Avoid: birth gender; birth sex; natal sex; born a woman; born a man; biologically female; biologically male; genetically female; genetically male; pre-op; post-op.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't play into gender essentialism or voyeuristic interest in bodies; avoid unnecessary mention of birth-assigned sex and be careful whether you need to discuss it at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating transgender people as though we have 'a condition.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: Monique is transgender; being transgender is not a crime. Use: gender dysphoria (when clinically relevant). Avoid: Monique has transgenderism; transsexualism/transsexuality is a sin; gender disordered; gender identity disorder (outdated); gender confused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize medical/psychiatric language properly and avoid pathologizing general trans existence; note recent diagnostic guideline revisions that remove disorder framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language that puts more value on being or appearing cisgender or that carries judgments around visibility.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: openly transgender; not openly transgender; perceived as cisgender. Avoid: passes; stealth; you’d never be able to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cis people should not use 'passing'/'stealth' unless asked; these terms imply deception. See note on 'out' and 'closeted' — disclosure is not the same as identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always use a person's correct name, pronouns (or lack thereof), and title/honorific.
rubrics_metrics.description: Always respect how a person refers to themself. Use examples with neopronouns and a variety of titles; avoid assuming honorifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names chosen by people are their real names (not 'nicknames' or 'aliases'); match pronouns and titles exactly; be aware of people preferring no title or uncommon titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a trans person's birth name or former pronouns without permission is a form of violence.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the person’s true/current name and pronouns even when writing about them in the past unless told otherwise. Avoid using birth name or former pronouns ('deadnaming').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be particularly careful in retrospective writing; do not 'out' people or use prior names/pronouns without explicit permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns are simply pronouns; they aren’t 'preferred' and aren’t inherently tied to gender identity or biology.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: pronouns; personal pronouns; she/her/hers; he/him/his; they/them/theirs; ze/zir/zirs; Sam/Sam/Sam. Avoid: preferred pronouns; masculine pronouns; feminine pronouns; male pronouns; female pronouns; non-binary pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat correct pronouns as required, not a preference. Avoid language that frames pronouns as optional 'preferences.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect singular they as a personal pronoun and use it appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use singular 'they' in personal and generic contexts: 'Elizabeth loves their cat; they are a big cat lover; they did something nice for themself yesterday.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major style guides and dictionaries endorse singular they; follow normal verb conjugation patterns (they did, they are). When using singular they, use reflexive 'themself' and follow examples in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the diversity of language people use to describe themselves.
rubrics_metrics.description: Find out what language an individual uses and never assume. Small differences (e.g., 'trans man' vs 'transman') can matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize individual self-identification over general style rules; when writing about groups be as descriptive and precise as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice particular sensitivity around culture-specific language related to gender identity and expression.
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that terms like Two Spirit, hijra, māhū, fa’afafine, and culture-specific labels have meanings that do not fully translate outside their contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand historical and cultural specificity before applying Western labels; avoid flattening or misapplying culturally embedded terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice particular sensitivity around bodies and anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid: female-bodied; male-bodied; biologically female/male; female/male organs. Use neutral/generic terms (genitals, reproductive organs, chest) and mirror the language people use for their own bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cis people should not use 'female-bodied'/'male-bodied' for others; be mindful that anatomy language can be triggering—especially for people with gender dysphoria. Medical providers should ask preferred terms and use generic language when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirm that trans women are women, trans men are men, and non-binary people are non-binary.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: all women, including trans women; cis and trans men; non-binary students; agender young adults. Avoid: women and trans women; normal people; real men; biological women; genetic men. Avoid phrasing that suggests a trans person 'identifies as' a gender when 'is' suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not linguistically separate trans people from cis people in a way that undermines identity. Avoid qualifiers like 'identifies as' where they would not be used for cis people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't sensationalize or nonconsensually disclose a trans person's gender history.
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person’s gender history isn’t relevant, don’t mention it. Never disclose birth name or assigned sex at birth without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize historical media harms; treat disclosure of history as potentially violent and avoid gossiping details. Use consent-driven reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use language that paints trans people as deceptive for living authentically.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases like: 'her secret was discovered'; 'he disguised himself as a woman'; 'she fooled everyone'; 'no one knew the truth'; 'the lie was exposed.' Instead use 'history', 'past', 'private', or 'nondisclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language implying deception has been used to justify violence (e.g., 'trans panic' defense); avoid wording that frames nondisclosure as lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't perpetuate or validate trans-exclusionary hate or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers have a moral obligation to do no harm and should not present anti-trans positions as equally valid or 'balanced' when they promote hate or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating prejudiced language and false equivalence in coverage (e.g., uncritically using terms like 'bathroom bill'); explicitly name trans-exclusionary movements and avoid euphemisms that sanitize harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating trans and intersex populations and invisibilizing intersex people.
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersex refers to atypical biological sex characteristics; transgender refers to gender identity misalignment with birth-assigned sex. They are separate but overlapping populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When topics relate to both groups, learn and explain intersex-specific needs rather than tacking 'intersex' on. Avoid rendering intersex people invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize more than two genders; use singular they in generic contexts and avoid gender-opposite framing.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inclusive generic language: 'each student must complete their homework; everyone; people of all/no genders.' Avoid 'men and women', 'the opposite sex', 'both genders', and constructions like 'his/her/they'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular they is grammatically defensible and endorsed by major guides; prefer 'they' over awkward multi-form constructions. Use wording that creates space for non-binary people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use LGBTQ (or variants) as a synonym for gay.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use: LGBTQ people versus non-LGBTQ people. Avoid: LGBTQ people versus straight people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using an umbrella acronym that includes trans people, ensure trans people are actually included in the context. Do not treat LGBTQ as synonymous with sexual orientation or 'gay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize 'queer' as a valid sexual orientation.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Queer' is a complex word with many definitions, and in trans communities many people identify as queer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor queer as a valid identity term where used; be attentive to context and history of the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple anatomy from identity.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conflating gendered identity terms with anatomy (e.g., avoid using 'women' as shorthand for all people who can menstruate). Use precise terms depending on context (e.g., 'pregnant people' when appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking anatomy and identity harms access and accuracy (research, medical services). In research reporting, be explicit about who was studied; if assumptions were made, note that as a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace that language evolves quickly.
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrate linguistic change as a reclaiming of agency by marginalized people rather than resist it; recognize rapid shifts and be open to learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guide as living guidance; stay humble and update language based on community usage and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize context, care, asking, and centering trans people as authorities.
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the guide as general guidance, not concrete rules. Focus on practicing care, consider context (medical vs social contexts, age, country), and consult trans people across identity lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the guide to police language or shame people; always ask individuals how they wish to be described and bring additional trans perspectives into editorial work.
